stories.topic: Why Bad Players Bet on Poker but Never on Chess
stories.summary: Ajay once asked Amit why weak players happily put money on poker but never on chess. Amit's answer: chess gives you feedback after every game, and Elo ratings on chess sites and in competitive chess are accurate, so everyone knows their level and a bad player won't bet against a better one. Poker is also a game of skill, but its variance is far higher. Every bad player gets lucky hands, lucky sessions, even lucky months, and many conclude they are good when they aren't.
stories.insight: Noise hides ability. Wherever luck is loud and feedback is slow, people mistake good fortune for skill. Good players guard against this by judging themselves on expected value rather than on short-term results.
stories.quote: Every bad player will have lucky hands, lucky sessions, even lucky months. And so many end up believing that they are good players when they are not. Poker can indeed be like a delusion machine.

stories.topic: Entitlement Tilt: When Doing It Right Makes You Play Wrong
stories.summary: The kind of tilt Amit was personally prone to was 'entitlement tilt'. He would sit down armed with math, game theory and a knowledge of ranges. Then a player who knew none of it, playing as if it were a festive card game, would hand him bad beats on hands he had played correctly. Amit would start fuming, play badly and lose money.
stories.insight: Knowing the correct play doesn't protect you from how you react to bad outcomes. Believing you deserve to win because you're doing things right is a trap of its own. The mental game is a separate skill from the math.
stories.quote: some idiot who knows none of this and is playing it like Teen Patti on Diwali would give me five bad beats in a hand and I played correctly, and suddenly I'd be fuming and I'd actually start playing badly and losing money.

stories.topic: Why the Winners Leave Poker and the Losers Stay
stories.summary: Amit played poker seriously from 2010 to 2015 and wrote a regular poker column for the Economic Times. When he started, he saw that only about 5% of players were long-term winners, and he assumed the winners would stay while the losers rotated out. By the time he left, he had realised the opposite was true. Winners leave because what makes them good at poker also makes them good at other things. Losers stay because they're addicted. He has seen lives destroyed by gambling addiction, and he warns anyone with an addictive personality not to play.
stories.insight: This is adverse selection over time. The people who can leave do, and the ecosystem fills up with those who can't. It also suggests that disciplined probabilistic thinking is a skill that carries over to other fields.
stories.quote: Many winning players leave because what makes them good at poker also makes them good at other things, so they move on. The losers stay because they're addicted.

core_ideas.concept: Expected Value: Separate the Decision from the Outcome
core_ideas.explanation: Amit starts with a fair coin. Heads, you win 51 paise; tails, you pay 49. Over 100 flips you'd expect to be up 100 paise, which is +1 paisa per flip, so taking the bet is 'plus-EV'. If it lands tails, you didn't decide badly; you got unlucky. The poker version: you hold ace-ten of hearts with a flush draw, which is about 38% to hit by the river. Your opponent shoves 10,000 into a 10,000 pot. You must call 10,000 to win 20,000, so you need to be right 33.3% of the time. That makes it an easy call. If he had bet 20,000 instead, you'd need 40%, and the right play is just about a fold. Keep making plus-EV decisions and you win in the long run.
core_ideas.quote: You made the right decision and you got unlucky.

core_ideas.concept: Pot Equity, Fold Equity, and Why Aggression Pays
core_ideas.explanation: Pot equity is your chance of winning multiplied by the size of the pot. Fold equity is what you collect when your raise makes the opponent give up. An all-in that loses money on raw winning chances can become plus-EV if the opponent folds half the time. So there are two reasons to bet: for value (to make a worse hand call) or as a bluff (to make a better hand fold). Implied odds stretch the same logic forward in time. Calling with a small pair can be worth it, even though you'll hit your third six only about one time in eight, if hitting it lets you extract much more money later. Since you never know an opponent's exact cards, all of this is calculated against the range of hands they might hold.
core_ideas.quote: You don't have to make the best hand to win. Making the other guy fold also works.

core_ideas.explanation: The dealer button moves one seat every hand, and the player on the button acts last. Acting later means you have already seen what everyone else did before you choose. That informational edge is so valuable that you can profitably play weaker and weaker hands the later your position. Part of a hand's value lies in when you get to decide, not just in the cards.
core_ideas.quote: The later your position in a hand, the more information you have about what the others are doing.

core_ideas.concept: Game Theory Optimal vs Exploitative Play
core_ideas.explanation: Suppose you bet 100 into a 200 pot on the river. Your opponent gets 3-to-1 on a call and needs to be right 25% of the time. If your betting range is exactly 25% bluffs and 75% value hands, you can't lose in the long run, whatever they hold or do. If they call too much or fold too much, you profit; if they play perfectly, you break even. For a pot-sized bet, the balanced mix is one-third bluffs. Real humans can't play this way consistently, so real poker is exploitative. You spot opponents' deviations: if they fold too much, you bluff more; if they call too much, you bet more for value. The same logic explains why the optimal strategy in rock-paper-scissors is pure randomness, and why both penalty-takers and goalkeepers must randomise.
core_ideas.quote: But equally when I am exploitative, I am also exploitable because I am also deviating from GTO.

core_ideas.concept: Tilt: Mastering the Math Isn't Enough
core_ideas.explanation: Tilt is a loss of composure, usually triggered by anger, that leads to bad decisions and lost money. Poker's emotional load is unusual. A bad day on March 15 can wipe out everything you won in January and February, especially since most players don't manage their bankroll. That can be devastating for men whose ego is tied to money as status and to winning. Loss aversion makes it worse, because a loss hurts more than an equal win pleases. There are many kinds of tilt, and you need to know which ones you're prone to.
core_ideas.quote: In theory, poker is all about the numbers. In practice, though, it's a mental game. Mastering the math is not enough. You also have to master the mind.

core_ideas.concept: Acknowledge Luck, Then Control the Controllable
core_ideas.explanation: This is Amit's first life lesson from poker. Poker is a game of skill, but the amount of luck in it is so large that the skill lies in managing that luck. Life is the same. Misreading luck has costs in both directions. Good fortune can make us arrogant and complacent, while bad fortune can make us defeatist or give us imposter syndrome. The answer is not fatalism. Accept what you can't control, focus only on what you can, and play the cards you're dealt as well as possible.
core_ideas.quote: I would go as far as to say that ninety eight or ninety nine percent of everything that happens to us is sheer luck.

core_ideas.concept: Don't Be Results-Oriented: Poker as a Route to Equanimity
core_ideas.explanation: Poker players are taught not to judge themselves by short-term results but by the quality of their process. Amit links this to the Gita: your dharma is to work hard and do the right thing, not to chase validation or the rewards you feel you're owed. Much of our unhappiness comes from not accepting consequences we don't control. Fully absorbing this produces a peaceful, almost Buddhist detachment from outcomes.
core_ideas.quote: In fact, the peaceful detachment can be so strong that one could argue that understanding poker is the route to Buddhism.

core_ideas.concept: Think Probabilistically and Beat Hindsight Bias
core_ideas.explanation: This is Amit's second life lesson. Hindsight bias makes everything in the past look inevitable. Once an event is over it either happened or it didn't. But beforehand, like a die still in the air, it was a set of probabilities. Seeing past decisions this way stops us blaming ourselves for good bets that went wrong. Putting rough numbers on important decisions also gives us clarity about what we are doing and why.
core_ideas.quote: after something has happened, it has 100% happened or it has zero percent happened, which means it's not happened.

core_ideas.explanation: When people dismiss poker as gambling, Amit gives two answers. First, it's a game of skill. Second, what's wrong with gambling? If gambling means acting on probabilistic judgements, we do it all day. Crossing the road carries a risk of being hit by a truck that is greater than the risk of an air accident. Approaching someone at a bar, buying a house and making a friend are all bets. Every action, with its opportunity costs, is a gamble. Most of us think probabilistically without admitting it; doing it openly helps us do it better.
core_ideas.quote: You buy a house, it's a gamble. You make a friend, it's a gamble.

core_ideas.concept: The Law of Truly Large Numbers
core_ideas.explanation: In his column 'Unlikely is Inevitable', Amit explains that with enough iterations, the most unlikely things will happen. So when terrible things happen to us, it isn't fate or the universe conspiring against us; it is how probability works over a long life. Ajay gives a personal version from years of walking in the mountains.
core_ideas.quote: if you spend ten to twenty days walking in the mountains for forty-five years. Then you know you're probably going to break your ankle once. So just the God of probability at work.

core_ideas.concept: Many Small 51% Bets Beat One Big Conviction Bet
core_ideas.explanation: Ajay applies this to finance, citing what he believes is Mark Twain's line: 'if you must forecast, forecast often'. The common mistake is to stay cautious and only commit when you feel absolutely sure, which he calls a delusion. Efficient markets theory says markets know a lot and pricing mistakes are small, so even reaching 51% accuracy is hard. Many small positions, each with a 51% chance, will work out better than one giant position held with full conviction.
core_ideas.quote: It is better to try to get to 51%. If you're going to be correct 51% of the time and you lay a large number of bets, then that's going to work for you.

core_ideas.concept: Independence and the Illusion of Diversification
core_ideas.explanation: Ajay points out a hidden requirement. The law of large numbers only works if the draws are independent. In poker, shuffling guarantees that. In finance it does not, because a single mindset can make a hundred apparently separate bets all flow from one correlated idea. You then believe you're diversified when you aren't. So you need many genuinely different ideas, each with a 51% edge.
core_ideas.quote: So what you can control is the number of ideas. And the extent to which they're correlated. The rest is up to Lady Luck, and then you just should be zen about it.

core_ideas.explanation: This is Amit's third life lesson. A single hand between the world's best player and a beginner is roughly 51-49, so the edge only shows up over a large sample. Poker players call building that sample 'putting in volume'. Every decision should aim to be plus-EV, and you must stay self-critical, because your assumptions or math may be wrong. For creators, volume pays twice. Constant iteration makes you better, and each new piece is another chance at a breakthrough idea or a viral hit. This doesn't mean spreading yourself across everything, which Amit calls daft; it means putting volume into what you're passionate about.
core_ideas.quote: if you have many doors, opportunity will knock somewhere or the other.

core_ideas.concept: The Tragic Asymmetry: Life Doesn't Give You a Million Hands
core_ideas.explanation: In poker you can play a million hands; Amit used to play several tables at once online. In many areas of life you can't build that kind of sample. Amit notes that he and Ajay were dealt incredibly good starting hands, and that their dharma is to make the most of them and help others. Ajay's response: where a large sample isn't an option, be zen. Don't beat yourself up, don't rage against the world, accept those lotteries and make the best of them.
core_ideas.quote: The tragic lesson of poker is that mostly everything is luck, and your skill only applies to how well you play the cards that you're dealt.

jokes_and_cultural_references.content: The opening spar. Ajay says listeners think 'we're some dull people that keep trying to feed you one obscure episode after another', and that 'one of us is a genius' at poker. Amit replies: 'I object to this. First of all, nobody thinks we're dull people... at least everybody in the comments seems to love us.' Then: 'the golden rule is that you underpromise and overdeliver. You are over promising by saying I'm a genius.'

On entitlement tilt, Amit describes the opponent who ruins his math-perfect game: 'some idiot who knows none of this and is playing it like Teen Patti on Diwali'. Teen Patti is the casual card game played at Diwali.

Amit on not being results-oriented: 'Lord Krishna and Spike Lee would be in agreement over this. Do the right thing, don't worry about the fruits of your action.' The line pairs the Gita's teaching on action with Spike Lee's film title.
Ajay cites Mark Twain ('I think') as saying 'if you must forecast, forecast often', and uses it to argue for many small bets over rare high-conviction ones.

On skill vs luck: Amit would lose all of a hundred tennis points to Nadal and a hundred chess games to Magnus Carlsen, 'even though I'm a good recreational player'. But a hand of poker between the world's best player and 'someone who just learned the rules, maybe someone who just watched my presentation' is about 51-49.

Game theory beyond poker: in rock-paper-scissors the optimal strategy is to be totally random. In football penalties, good goalkeepers know the taker's stats, so good takers randomise, which forces goalkeepers to randomise too.

Last year's World Series of Poker Main Event, the de facto world championship: a $10,000 entry fee, 60,000 starting tournament chips, blinds climbing from 100/200 to millions, a prize pool of around $95 million and a first prize of about $12 million. Amit uses it to illustrate how tournaments work.
Amit says films and popular culture 'completely get it wrong'. They make poker look like a game of spotting tells and bluffs, when the foundation is math and game theory.

Amit's legal caveat for Indian readers: when he last checked, live poker was possible only in Goa's offshore casinos and in Sikkim. Online poker is legal in most states, but check for yourself before playing.
The deadpan ending. Picking up on Ajay's advice not to beat yourself up, Amit muses aloud: 'How does somebody beat themselves up?' After a pause from Ajay, he signs off: 'next time.'
